chunks.text: A tourniquet should be applied 2-3 inches above the wound on the limb, never over a joint. Tighten until bleeding stops completely. Write the time of application on the tourniquet or skin using a marker. Do not remove the tourniquet once applied in the field — this decision is made by a medical officer only. Common Indian Army tourniquet: CAT (Combat Application Tourniquet). If no tourniquet is available, improvise with a belt or cloth and a stick to twist and tighten (windlass method).

For deep wounds where a tourniquet cannot be applied (e.g., groin, armpit, neck), pack the wound tightly with gauze or a hemostatic dressing. Push gauze deep into the cavity and apply firm continuous pressure for at least 3-5 minutes. Do not remove packing in the field. Hemostatic agents like QuikClot or HemCon may be issued to soldiers. After packing, apply a pressure dressing on top to maintain pressure.

A tension pneumothorax occurs when air accumulates in the chest cavity, collapsing the lung. Signs include: difficulty breathing, absent breath sounds on one side, trachea shifted away from the affected side, dropping blood pressure, distended neck veins. Treatment in the field: needle decompression at the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line using a 14G needle. A chest seal (vented) should be applied to any open chest wound to prevent this condition.

Soldiers are at risk of hypothermia in high-altitude postings like Siachen, Ladakh, or Kashmir. Symptoms progress: shivering (mild), confusion and loss of coordination (moderate), no shivering with altered consciousness (severe). Prevention: never sleep in wet clothes, use layered clothing systems, carry an emergency space blanket, eat high-calorie food regularly, stay hydrated. Treatment: remove wet clothing, insulate the casualty from the ground, apply warmth to the core (armpits, groin, neck), never rub the extremities.

For burns sustained from vehicle fires, IED blasts, or incendiary weapons: do not apply toothpaste, oil, or ice — these worsen injury. Cool the burn with clean cool (not cold) water for 20 minutes. Cover with a clean non-adhesive dressing. Elevate the affected area. Assess burn depth: superficial (redness), partial thickness (blisters), full thickness (white/charred, no pain). Burns covering more than 20% body surface area require immediate evacuation. Inhalation burns (singed nasal hair, hoarse voice) are life-threatening.

AMS occurs when ascending above 2,500m too quickly. Symptoms: headache, nausea, dizziness, fatigue, poor sleep. The most important rule is: never ascend with symptoms. Treatment: descend 300-500m, rest, hydration, Paracetamol or Ibuprofen for headache. Acetazolamide (Diamox) is used for prevention — 125-250mg twice daily starting 1-2 days before ascent. Indian Army postings in Ladakh, Kargil, and Arunachal Pradesh require mandatory acclimatization periods.

HAPE is a life-threatening accumulation of fluid in the lungs at altitude. It is the leading cause of death from altitude illness. Symptoms: breathlessness at rest, dry cough progressing to pink frothy sputum, crackling sound in lungs, cyanosis (blue lips/fingertips). HAPE can develop with or without prior AMS. Immediate treatment: descend at least 1000m urgently, administer supplemental oxygen, Nifedipine 30mg extended release if available. Do not let the casualty exert themselves during descent.

HACE is brain swelling due to altitude and is the most severe form of altitude illness. Symptoms: severe headache unresponsive to analgesics, loss of coordination (ataxia — cannot walk a straight line), confusion, altered consciousness, seizures, coma. Ataxia test: ask the soldier to walk heel-to-toe in a straight line. Any difficulty is a red flag. Immediate treatment: descend urgently, supplemental oxygen, Dexamethasone 8mg immediately then 4mg every 6 hours. Hyperbaric bag (Gamow bag) is life-saving if available.

Heat Exhaustion: heavy sweating, weakness, cold/pale/clammy skin, fast weak pulse, nausea, fainting. Core temperature usually below 40°C. Treatment: move to cool area, loosen clothing, apply cool wet cloths, hydrate with ORS. Heat Stroke: high body temperature (above 40°C), hot/red/dry or damp skin, rapid strong pulse, confusion, unconsciousness. This is a medical emergency. Treatment: call for evacuation, rapidly cool the casualty by any means — ice packs to neck/armpits/groin, cool water sponging, fan. Heat stroke can cause permanent organ damage and death if not treated immediately.

Malaria is a serious risk in jungle postings — Northeast India, Andaman Islands, and border areas. Caused by Plasmodium parasites via Anopheles mosquito bites (mostly at night). Symptoms: high fever with chills and sweating in cycles, headache, muscle aches, vomiting. Falciparum malaria (most dangerous type) can cause cerebral malaria, kidney failure, and death. Prevention: use DEET-based insect repellent, permethrin-treated uniforms, sleep under mosquito nets, take prophylactic medication as prescribed. Report any fever after jungle exposure immediately to medical staff.

India has the highest snakebite mortality in the world. Venomous snakes soldiers may encounter: King Cobra, Indian Cobra, Common Krait, Russell's Viper, Saw-Scaled Viper. Signs of envenomation: local swelling and pain (viper), drooping eyelids and difficulty swallowing (cobra/krait), bleeding from gums. Do NOT: cut and suck the wound, apply tourniquet, apply electric shock. DO: immobilize the limb below heart level, keep the casualty calm, mark the edge of swelling and time, evacuate urgently to a facility with antivenom. Pressure immobilization bandage is only recommended for neurotoxic snakes (cobra, krait).

Scrub typhus is increasingly common in Indian troops posted in forested areas. Caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, transmitted by larval mites (chiggers). A classic sign is an eschar — a painless black scab at the bite site, often in hidden areas (groin, armpit, behind ear). Symptoms: sudden high fever, severe headache, rash, enlarged lymph nodes. Untreated, it can cause pneumonia, encephalitis, and organ failure. Treatment: Doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 7-14 days. Always check for eschar during medical examination after jungle operations.

The INSAS (Indian Small Arms System) is the standard infantry rifle of the Indian Army. Caliber: 5.56x45mm NATO. Effective range: 400m (point target), 600m (area target). Magazine capacity: 20 or 30 rounds. Modes: single shot and 3-round burst (no fully automatic). Function check: remove magazine, cock weapon, press trigger (should release), apply safety, press trigger (should not release), decock. Common malfunction: double feed — clear by removing magazine, pulling charging handle twice, visually inspect chamber, reload.

The AK-203 is being inducting into Indian Army replacing the INSAS. Caliber: 7.62x39mm. Effective range: 400m. Magazine: 30 rounds. Fully automatic capable. Manufactured at Amethi under Indo-Russian joint venture. The AK platform is known for reliability in adverse conditions including sand, mud, and extreme cold — suitable for Ladakh and desert operations. Malfunction clearance (immediate action): tap the magazine, rack the charging handle, observe the chamber, release the bolt, squeeze the trigger (TROSS drills).

The Dragunov SVD is the primary sniper rifle in Indian Army service. Caliber: 7.62x54mmR. Effective range: 800m (with optical sight), 1300m (maximum). Magazine: 10 rounds, semi-automatic. Equipped with PSO-1 telescopic sight with rangefinder reticle and infrared filter for detecting IR sources. Used extensively in counter-insurgency operations in J&K and counter-sniper roles along the LOC. Windage and elevation adjustments critical for high-altitude engagements due to thinner air and changed ballistics.

The IWI NEGEV LMG is used by Indian Army special forces and some infantry units. Caliber: 5.56x45mm. Belt fed or magazine. Rate of fire: 850-1000 rpm cyclic. Effective range: 1000m. The LMG provides suppressive fire to allow the rifle section to maneuver. Key principles: the LMG gunner should control burst length (5-7 round bursts) to prevent barrel overheating and maintain accuracy. Barrel changes are mandatory after sustained fire.

The Carl Gustaf (84mm) is a man-portable anti-armor and multi-role weapon used extensively by Indian Army infantry. It fires multiple warhead types: HEAT (anti-armor), HE (anti-personnel), ILLUM (illumination), SMOKE, and HEDP. Effective range: 300m vs armor, 700m vs area targets. Backblast danger zone: 100m arc, 60 degrees behind the weapon — never position personnel or flammable materials here. The Carl Gustaf was extensively used in the 1999 Kargil War against Pakistani bunkers.

The 81mm mortar provides indirect fire support at the battalion level. Maximum range: 5,650m. Minimum range: 100m. Rate of fire: 15 rounds per minute (sustained: 4 rpm). Crew: 3-4 soldiers. Components: barrel, bipod, baseplate, sight. Key safety: misfired round — wait 2 minutes, then carefully extract (never look down the barrel). The mortar is the infantry battalion commander's closest artillery support. Used for suppression, illumination, and smoke missions.

Topographic maps used by Indian Army are typically at 1:50,000 scale (2cm = 1km on ground). Grid references: 6-digit (100m accuracy), 8-digit (10m accuracy), 10-digit (1m accuracy). Always read grid references: RIGHT then UP (Easting then Northing). Contour lines show elevation — closer lines mean steeper terrain. Index contours (darker, labeled) appear every 5th line. A closed set of contours forming a circle indicates a hilltop. A 'V' shape in contours pointing uphill indicates a valley; pointing downhill indicates a ridge.

The prismatic compass is standard issue in the Indian Army. Magnetic bearing: reading from compass. Grid bearing: reading from map. Magnetic declination in India varies by region (check map margin). Converting map bearing to compass bearing: add the magnetic declination if west, subtract if east. Resection: take bearings to two or more known landmarks, plot back bearings on map — your position is where the lines intersect. Always check compass away from metal objects, weapons, and electronic equipment which cause deviation.

The Indian Army uses GPS receivers and increasingly NAVIC (Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System). Key skills: entering waypoints, tracking to a destination, understanding accuracy limitations (especially in deep jungle or mountainous terrain where satellite view is obstructed). Battery conservation: GPS should supplement, not replace map and compass skills. In electronic warfare environments, GPS may be jammed — soldiers must be confident in traditional navigation. MGRS (Military Grid Reference System) is the standard coordinate format for military GPS.

Effective camouflage disrupts shape, shine, shadow, silhouette, and movement (5 S's). Shine: camouflage cream on all exposed skin, dull metallic parts with tape or cam cream. Shape: break up outline by adding local vegetation to helmet and clothing. Shadow: avoid standing in doorways or against light backgrounds. Silhouette: never stand on skylines. Movement: slow deliberate movement, freeze when in doubt, move at dusk or night when possible. In snow terrain (Ladakh, Siachen): white over-suits mandatory, avoid dark shadows cast by the body.

Indian Army patrol orders follow the SMEAC format: Situation (enemy and friendly forces), Mission (clear concise statement beginning with 'To' and containing who, what, where, when, why), Execution (scheme of maneuver, tasks to subordinates, coordinating instructions), Administration & Logistics (casualty evacuation, resupply, communications), Command & Signal (chain of command, radio frequencies, codewords, challenge and password). Rehearsals must cover Actions-on: enemy contact, casualty, getting lost, compromise.

On ambush: if caught in the killing zone — assault through or extract, do not freeze. Battle drills: section attack — Locate, Win the firefight, Attack, Consolidate (LWAC). On contact, the section commander shouts 'CONTACT!' followed by direction using clock method ('Contact 11 o'clock!'). Fire and movement: one group fires while the other moves — bounding overwatch. Never all move at the same time. On breaking contact: peel drill — last man fires, taps the shoulder of the man in front, moves to the rear, and the drill continues.

Hydration is critical — dehydration degrades performance significantly before thirst is felt. Sources: streams, rain, dew, plant water. Signs of contamination: cloudy water, dead animals nearby, discolored vegetation. Purification methods: boiling (100°C for 1 minute, 3 minutes above 2000m altitude), iodine/chlorine tablets (issued in field kit, wait 30 minutes), water purification filters. Soldier's water consumption: minimum 2-3L/day in temperate conditions, 4-6L/day in desert or heavy exertion. Never share canteens — risk of disease transmission.

In a survival situation, food is less critical than water and shelter — a fit soldier can survive 3 weeks without food. Universal edibility test: touch plant to lips (wait 15 min), chew without swallowing (wait 15 min), eat small amount and wait 8 hours — proceed if no ill effects. Avoid: brightly colored plants, plants with milky sap, plants that smell of almonds (cyanide indicator), any mushrooms unless 100% certain. In India: coconut, bamboo shoots, roots of cattail, and most fruits that animals are seen eating are generally safe.

Priority order in survival: Protection, Location, Water, Food (PLWF). Shelter protects from hypothermia, hyperthermia, and insects. Types: lean-to (simplest — requires only one upright support and covering material), A-frame, debris hut (mound of leaves providing insulation — effective in cold environments). Site selection: avoid flood plains, ant nests, dead wood above that could fall, areas with large animal tracks. Insulate from the ground — ground steals body heat 25x faster than air.

Standard Indian Army radio procedure: Call sign of station called, then own call sign, then message, then 'Over' (reply expected) or 'Out' (conversation ended — never 'Over and Out'). Phonetic alphabet (NATO): Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India, Juliet, Kilo, Lima, Mike, November, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, Uniform, Victor, Whiskey, X-ray, Yankee, Zulu. Numbers spoken digit by digit (e.g., 37 = 'Three Seven'). Radio silence: maintain unless operationally essential.

Operational Security (OPSEC): Never transmit unit strength, location, or future plans in clear (unencrypted). Avoid patterns in communications that can be exploited by signals intelligence. Mobile phone use near operational areas is restricted — smartphones can reveal location through GPS metadata and towers. Social media posting of operational information is strictly prohibited and a punishable offense. Enemy SIGINT (Signals Intelligence) units actively monitor frequencies. Use encrypted radios (AREN series in Indian Army) for all sensitive communications.

The BMP-2 Sarath is the primary infantry fighting vehicle (IFV) of the Indian Army, manufactured indigenously at Ordnance Factory Medak. It carries up to 7 infantry soldiers plus 3 crew. Armament: 30mm 2A42 autocannon, 7.62mm PKT coaxial machine gun, Konkurs ATGM launcher. It is amphibious — can cross water obstacles by swimming. Crew roles: commander, gunner, driver. The driver uses periscopes in closed-down mode. Soldiers must know emergency exit procedures from all hatches.

The T-90 Bhishma is the primary Main Battle Tank (MBT) of the Indian Army. Over 1,000 in service. Armament: 125mm smoothbore gun (can fire APFSDS, HEAT, and Refleks ATGM through barrel), 7.62mm coaxial MG, 12.7mm anti-aircraft MG. Engine: 1000hp diesel. Speed: 60 km/h road, 35 km/h off-road. Crew: 3 (commander, gunner, driver). Features: Kontakt-5 explosive reactive armor (ERA), Shtora active protection system. The T-90 was deployed extensively in Rajasthan desert operations and along northern borders.

Operators must conduct daily PMCS (Preventive Maintenance Checks and Services). Daily checks: fuel level, coolant level, oil level, battery terminals, tyre pressure, lights, brake check. If a vehicle is immobilized in combat: push it off the road if possible, mark its location on map, report up the chain, do not abandon it without authorization. Common field recovery: tow ropes, snatch blocks for mechanical advantage, sand channels for soft ground recovery. Never attempt to work under a vehicle supported only by a jack — use stands.

Searching personnel in counter-insurgency: always have two soldiers — one searches, one covers with weapon ready. Search from head to toe: hat/turban, collar, torso, waistband, pockets, crotch area, down both legs, footwear. All jewelry and belt items checked. Vehicle search: engine bay, under chassis, door panels, beneath seats, spare tyre, fuel tank area. Never take eyes off the person being searched. Common IED concealment: inside walls, under road surface, inside animals, buried under culverts.

A cordon and search isolates a target area while a search party enters. Key elements: Outer cordon (prevents escape or reinforcement), Inner cordon (immediate perimeter of target building), Search party (systematic search of buildings), Reserve (ready to reinforce). Sequence: establish outer cordon covertly, move inner cordon into position, search party enters. Timing: often pre-dawn (0300-0500) to maximize surprise. All personnel accounted for before withdrawal. Lessons from Kashmir operations: always check rooftops, tunnels, and false walls.

Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs) are the primary threat in counter-insurgency. Indicators: disturbed earth, unusual objects on road (stones, plastic bags, wire), dead animals, parked vehicles unattended. Command wire IEDs: look for wire running away from road into vegetation. Vehicle-Borne IEDs (VBIEDs): suspect any vehicle parked unusually or abandoned. On suspected IED: stop, assess, report, keep clear (minimum 300m), inform EOD. Avoid using radios within 25m — can trigger radio-controlled IEDs. Cordon the area and wait for EOD.

The 1999 Kargil War highlighted several tactical lessons. Pakistani forces occupied high-ground features in Dras, Batalik, Mushkoh, and Kaksar sectors. Key lessons: importance of all-weather surveillance and aerial reconnaissance, danger of predictable patrol routes, need for dedicated high-altitude warfare training, critical role of artillery (Bofors guns decisive), need for night-vision equipment. Indian Army's Totak feature and Tiger Hill operations demonstrated successful combined arms coordination. Siachin experience proved vital for troops adapted to extreme altitude.

NBC (Nuclear, Biological, Chemical) threats require protective equipment: NBC suit, gloves, and S10 or similar respirator. Decontamination drill: remove contaminated clothing (careful not to touch skin), rinse skin with large amounts of water, proceed to decontamination station. Nerve agent signs: small pupils (miosis), excessive saliva, sweating, muscle twitching, seizures. Antidote: Atropine auto-injector (inject into outer thigh through clothing in emergency). Blister agent (mustard): no immediate pain — symptoms appear 2-24 hours later, causing blisters and eye damage.

Detection methods in Indian Army include: M8 paper (turns yellow-green for nerve/blister agents), M9 tape (turns pink/red/red-purple in presence of liquid agents), electronic detectors. Water test for blister agents: drop water on suspected area — mustard forms a distinct oily bead. On first suspicion of chemical attack: immediately don mask, give alarm (three blasts on whistle, shout 'Gas! Gas! Gas!'), don gloves and suit in correct order. Do not remove mask until cleared by NBC NCO with detection equipment.

The Army Act 1950 governs the Indian Army. Key sections relevant to soldiers: Section 39 (absence without leave), Section 40 (desertion), Section 41 (striking a superior officer), Section 45 (disgraceful conduct), Section 63 (prejudice to military discipline — residual clause). Punishment types: Summary punishment (awarded by Commanding Officer) and Court Martial (General, District, Summary General, Summary). Soldiers have the right to submit a complaint through the chain of command under Army Rules 177. Redressal mechanism: complaint to CO, then formation commander, then Army Headquarters.

Promotion in Indian Army for Other Ranks (ORs): Recruit to Sepoy (on completion of training), Sepoy to Naik (by selection/time scale after minimum service), Naik to Havildar, Havildar to Naib Subedar (JCO — major promotion gate), Naib Subedar to Subedar, Subedar to Subedar Major (highest JCO rank). Annual Confidential Reports (ACRs) are critical. Physical fitness tests (including running, pull-ups, and combat fitness) are mandatory for promotion boards. LDMC (Lower Divisional Military Course) and other qualifying courses are required.

Key welfare schemes for soldiers and veterans: ECHS (Ex-Servicemen Contributory Health Scheme) — healthcare for ESM and dependents at ECHS polyclinics and empanelled hospitals. Canteen Stores Department (CSD) — subsidized goods. OROP (One Rank One Pension) — uniform pension for same rank and service. Sainik Boards at district, state, and central level for welfare issues. Army Wives Welfare Association (AWWA). PM Scholarship for children of deceased/disabled soldiers. Veterans India portal for online grievance redressal.

In the event of a soldier becoming a casualty: immediate informing of unit Adjutant, who informs the Commanding Officer. Official communication to family via Record Office — do not allow unofficial information to reach family first. Battle casualty: ex-gratia payment, pension continuation, disability pension (if applicable). Next of Kin (NOK) details must be kept updated in service documents. If a soldier dies in action, the family receives Veer Nari (war widow) status with associated benefits including priority government housing.

chunks.text: Combat stress is a normal response to abnormal situations. Immediate stress reactions (during/just after combat): confusion, trembling, tears, aggression. Delayed reactions (weeks-months later): flashbacks, nightmares, hypervigilance, emotional numbing, avoidance — this is Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). The Indian Army increasingly has formal mental health support through NIMHANS collaboration and unit medical officers. It is NOT a sign of weakness — it is a physiological injury. Soldiers experiencing these symptoms must report to the MO. Early treatment significantly improves outcomes.

The Indian Army has a Buddy System where soldiers are paired to watch out for each other's mental and physical wellbeing. Warning signs a buddy may need help: giving away possessions, saying goodbye in a final way, sudden calmness after depression, withdrawal from unit activities, dramatic mood changes, talking about feeling worthless. Action: engage in conversation, listen without judgment, immediately inform the section commander and MO — this is the correct action, not a betrayal. All such cases are handled with confidentiality.

Nuclear detonation hazards: blast, heat, initial radiation, fallout (residual radiation). Protective measures: distance (most effective), shielding (dense materials — concrete, earth, lead absorb gamma), time (reduce exposure duration). In a fallout area: stay indoors in brick/concrete building, seal gaps with wet cloth, switch off ventilation, remove outer clothing before entering shelter (removes 80% of contamination). Dosimetry: radiation dose measured in mSv/Gy. Army issues personal dosimeters to track cumulative dose. KI (Potassium Iodide) tablets protect thyroid from radioactive iodine — only effective if taken before or just after exposure.

Basic mountaineering skills are essential for high-altitude operations in Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, and Uttarakhand. Rappelling (abseiling): controlled descent on rope. Key knots: Figure-8 (anchor), Bowline (harness tie-in), Clove hitch (quick attachment), Prussik (self-arrest). Three points of contact always maintained when climbing. Belay system: one person always anchored and protecting the climber. Equipment: carabiners, belay devices, harness, helmet, pitons. The High Altitude Warfare School (HAWS) at Gulmarg trains soldiers in these skills.

Avalanche risk is constant in Siachen, Kargil, and high-altitude postings — the Indian Army loses more soldiers to avalanches annually than to enemy action. High-risk conditions: recent heavy snowfall (within 24 hours), temperature rise, wind-loaded slopes, convex slope features, previous avalanche debris. If caught in an avalanche: discard equipment, fight to stay on surface (swimming motion), cover mouth with arm as snow settles, create an air pocket before snow stops, try to push hand to surface. Bury a glove as marker. Rescue: buried victims have 90% survival if found in 15 minutes, dropping rapidly after 45 minutes.

Room clearing is a dangerous task requiring precision. Four-man team standard: number 1 and 2 make entry (cross immediately to opposite corners), number 3 and 4 follow to clear remaining corners. Never stack against the door (fatal funnel). Grenade: shout 'GRENADE!' before throwing into room, take cover, enter after detonation — 'Clear!' call. Pie the door: incrementally clear visible area before entry. Clearing direction: always work from the dominant corner. Communicate constantly: 'Covering left!', 'Moving right!', 'Room clear!'. In Indian context practiced extensively for Kashmir counter-insurgency operations.

FIBUA (Fighting In Built-Up Areas) principles: move along walls not across open streets, use shadows, avoid windows (silhouette danger), use multiple routes, communicate with hand signals when possible. Rooftops: valuable observation but dangerous — silhouette against sky. Breach: door (kick, ram, explosive), wall (sledgehammer, C2 explosive, vehicle). Dominate the high ground — control of upper floors is critical. Civilian presence: strict ROE (Rules of Engagement) must be followed. Collateral damage prevention is operational, legal, and moral imperative. Lessons from Srinagar operations extensively documented by Indian Army.

Important battles and operations in Indian Army history: Battle of Longewala (1971) — small force held Pakistan armor with air support (basis of movie Border). Operation Vijay (1961) — Goa liberation. Operation Blue Star (1984) — Golden Temple. Operation Pawan (1987-1990) — Sri Lanka IPKF. Operation Vijay (1999) — Kargil War. Operation Parakram (2001-2002) — mobilization after Parliament attack. Operation Rakshak — ongoing counter-insurgency J&K. PVC (Param Vir Chakra) — India's highest gallantry award, equivalent to Victoria Cross/Medal of Honor.

Indian Army ranks from lowest to highest: Sepoy/Gunner/Sapper/Trooper, Lance Naik, Naik, Havildar, Naib Subedar (JCO), Subedar (JCO), Subedar Major/Risaldar Major (JCO), 2nd Lieutenant, Lieutenant, Captain, Major, Lieutenant Colonel, Colonel, Brigadier, Major General, Lieutenant General, General, Field Marshal (honorary, wartime). JCOs (Junior Commissioned Officers) are a unique Indian Army institution — senior to soldiers but subordinate to commissioned officers. They are the backbone of the regiment.

A standard Indian Army infantry battalion has approximately 850 soldiers. Structure: Battalion HQ, HQ Company, 4 Rifle Companies (Alpha/Bravo/Charlie/Delta). Each Rifle Company: Company HQ + 3 Platoons. Each Platoon: Platoon HQ + 3 Sections. Each Section: 10 soldiers (Section Commander + 9 soldiers). Support elements: Mortar Platoon, Anti-Tank Platoon, Signal Platoon, Pioneer Platoon, Reconnaissance Platoon. Commanding Officer is a Colonel; Company Commanders are Majors; Platoon Commanders are Lieutenants or 2nd Lieutenants.

Unconscious breathing casualty: place in recovery position (on their side, upper knee bent forward to prevent rolling, lower arm behind, upper arm supporting head). This prevents choking on vomit or blood. Airway obstruction: look (chest rise), listen (breath sounds), feel (air on cheek). If obstructed: head tilt-chin lift, jaw thrust (if spinal injury suspected). Choking (conscious): 5 back blows between shoulder blades, then 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver). If unconscious: begin CPR. Jaw thrust is used in trauma as it does not move the cervical spine.

Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) for a soldier with no pulse and not breathing: 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths (30:2 ratio). Compression depth: at least 5cm (2 inches), at the center of the chest. Rate: 100-120 compressions per minute (tempo: 'Stayin' Alive'). Allow full chest recoil. If untrained or reluctant: compression-only CPR (no mouth-to-mouth) is effective. Continue CPR until: casualty regains pulse and breathing, trained medical personnel take over, you are too exhausted to continue, or evacuation to definitive care. AED use: apply pads as shown in diagram, follow voice prompts.

Radio sets commonly used in Indian Army: AREN (Army Radio Engineered Net) series — secure encrypted tactical radios. Harris RF-7800 — software defined radio, used by special forces. Motorola TETRA radios — for peacekeeping and urban ops. VHF radios: line-of-sight, 30-300MHz, range 10-20km depending on terrain. HF radios: can communicate over the horizon using skywave propagation, 3-30MHz, used for long-range communication. BFSR-SR and other battlefield surveillance radars also have associated communication. Always check battery level, antenna connection, and frequency before operation.

chunks.text: Indian Army field rations (composite rations) provide approximately 3,600-4,200 kcal per day for medium-intensity operations (4,500+ kcal for high-altitude and cold weather). Components: carbohydrates (main fuel — chapati, rice, biscuits), proteins (dal, meat products), fats, vitamins. At altitude, appetite is naturally suppressed — soldiers must be encouraged/ordered to eat. Dehydration mimics altitude sickness — drink before you feel thirsty. Avoid alcohol at altitude as it accelerates dehydration and impairs judgment. Hot rations boost morale significantly.

CASEVAC (Casualty Evacuation) is the movement of casualties from point of injury to medical facility. 9-Line MEDEVAC request: Line 1-Location (grid), Line 2-Radio frequency/callsign, Line 3-Number of patients by precedence (P1 Urgent, P2 Priority, P3 Routine), Line 4-Special equipment needed, Line 5-Number by type (litter/ambulatory), Line 6-Security at pickup site, Line 7-Method of marking, Line 8-Patient nationality and status, Line 9-NBC contamination. In Indian Army, Dhruv helicopter (ALH-MR) is primary CASEVAC platform in high-altitude areas.

India shares borders with Pakistan (3,323 km), China (3,488 km — Line of Actual Control), Bangladesh (4,156 km), Nepal (1,751 km), Bhutan (699 km), Myanmar (1,643 km), and a maritime boundary with Sri Lanka and Maldives. Key contested areas: LOC (Line of Control) with Pakistan in J&K, LAC (Line of Actual Control) with China in Ladakh/Arunachal Pradesh. The Siachen Glacier is the world's highest battlefield at 5,400m average elevation. Depsang, Galwan, Pangong Tso, and Daulat Beg Oldie are key areas of concern along LAC.

Night Vision Devices (NVDs) used by Indian Army include image intensifier (Gen 2 and Gen 3) goggles and monoculars, and thermal imaging sights. Image intensifiers amplify available light — not effective in complete darkness. Thermal imagers detect heat signature — effective in all light conditions. Key limitations: NVDs impair depth perception and narrow field of view — soldiers must be trained to compensate. Battery life critical — always carry spare batteries. Care: never expose NVDs to bright light when switched on, keep dry and free of lens condensation. IRGSU (Individual Rifle Grenade Sight Unit) and BEL-made products are Indian.

Rules of Engagement (ROE) are directives from military authority that define when, where, and how force may be used. In J&K operations, soldiers operate under AFSPA (Armed Forces Special Powers Act) which grants specific powers in disturbed areas. Key principle: force must be necessary and proportionate. Escalation of Force (EOF): shout warning, show weapon, non-lethal warning (flare/warning shot), lethal force — only if threat to life is imminent. Any use of lethal force must be reported up the chain immediately. Weapon must not be fired in anger — always an ordered act.

Eye injuries are common in blast and fragmentation incidents. Types: corneal abrasion (foreign body in eye — do not rub, irrigate with clean water, patch both eyes as eyes move together), penetrating eye injury (do not remove object, cover with rigid shield — NOT pressure bandage, evacuate urgently), flash blindness (temporary from explosions or laser — reassure, will recover in minutes to hours), chemical splash (irrigate immediately with large volumes of water for minimum 20 minutes). The golden rule for any serious eye injury: cover, do not compress, evacuate. Vision loss is permanent if penetrating injury is mishandled.

Fractures in field conditions must be stabilised before evacuation. Open fracture (bone visible): cover wound with clean dressing, do not push bone back, immobilise, give antibiotics if available (Amoxicillin-Clavulanate), evacuate urgently — infection risk is high. Closed fracture: immobilise joint above and below fracture using improvised splint (rifle, straight branch, rolled sleeping mat) padded with clothing. Check circulation, sensation, and movement (CSM) before and after splinting — pulse distal to fracture must be present. Femur fracture can cause 1-2 litres of internal blood loss — treat for shock.

Suspect spinal injury in: fall from height, vehicle rollover, blast injury, diving accident, any trauma with neck or back pain, or unconscious trauma patient. Do NOT bend, twist, or flex the spine. Log roll technique: minimum 3 people, one controls the head maintaining inline stabilisation, two roll the body as a unit. Improvised cervical collar: rolled sleeping mat or clothing around neck. Improvised stretcher: two rifles through sleeves of two jackets. Patient must be moved on a firm surface. Neurological signs: tingling, weakness, or paralysis in limbs after trauma — treat as spinal injury until proven otherwise.

Common medications carried at section or platoon level in Indian Army. Analgesics: Paracetamol 500mg (pain, fever — safe), Ibuprofen 400mg (pain, inflammation — avoid in dehydration/kidney disease), Morphine auto-injector (severe pain, trauma — causes respiratory depression, never give to head injury). Antibiotics: Amoxicillin (infections), Ciprofloxacin (diarrhoea, wound infection). Anti-malarials: Chloroquine or Primaquine (area-dependent). Anti-diarrhoeal: ORS (rehydration — always preferred over stopping diarrhoea with Loperamide in infection). Antacid: Omeprazole. All medications must be checked for allergy before administration.

IV fluids are administered in haemorrhagic shock when oral fluids are not possible. Types: Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl — replaces blood volume), Ringer's Lactate (preferred in trauma, more physiologically balanced), Dextrose 5% (for hypoglycaemia — not for fluid resuscitation). Permissive hypotension: in penetrating trauma, target systolic BP of 80-90 mmHg rather than normalising BP — prevents clot disruption. Signs of shock: rapid weak pulse, pale cold clammy skin, altered consciousness, reduced urine output. Two large-bore IV lines in antecubital fossa. Intraosseous (IO) route if IV access fails — drill into tibia.

Dengue is transmitted by Aedes mosquito (daytime biter unlike malaria mosquito). Symptoms: sudden high fever, severe headache, pain behind eyes, bone and joint pain (breakbone fever), rash (red with white islands), bleeding from gums or nose. Warning signs of severe dengue: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, rapid breathing, fatigue. No specific antiviral — treatment is supportive: paracetamol (NOT aspirin or ibuprofen — increases bleeding risk), oral rehydration, rest. Platelet monitoring critical. Evacuate if warning signs present. Prevention: DEET repellent effective against Aedes, remove stagnant water from camp area.

Leptospirosis is caused by Leptospira bacteria found in water contaminated by animal urine (rats, dogs, cattle). Common in flooding, waterlogged terrain after monsoon, and jungle operations. Entry: through cuts in skin or mucous membranes. Symptoms: sudden fever, severe muscle pain (especially calves), headache, red eyes (conjunctival suffusion), jaundice (yellow skin/eyes) in severe cases. Weil's disease (severe form): kidney failure, liver failure, bleeding. Prevention: waterproof boots, avoid wading in floodwater with open wounds, doxycycline prophylaxis in high-risk situations. Treatment: Doxycycline or Penicillin.

Cholera causes profuse rice-water diarrhoea and can kill through dehydration within hours. Caused by Vibrio cholerae in contaminated water. Field sanitation breakdown is the primary cause of outbreaks. ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) is life-saving — 1 litre water, 6 teaspoons sugar, half teaspoon salt. Zinc supplements reduce severity in children. Antibiotic (Doxycycline or Azithromycin) reduces duration. Prevention: only drink purified water, cook food thoroughly, wash hands after defecation and before eating. Camp sanitation: latrines minimum 30m downwind and downhill from water source and 30m from cookhouse.

An Observation Post (OP) provides continuous surveillance of a designated area. OP routine: observer and sentry rotate every 30-60 minutes to prevent fatigue-induced errors. Systematic observation: use binoculars, scan from ground to horizon, near to far, left to right in overlapping arcs. Recording: maintain OP log with time, grid, description, and direction of all activity. Reporting: use SALUTE format — Size, Activity, Location, Uniform/Unit, Time, Equipment. Camouflage of OP: no movement during daylight in exposed positions, no smoking, no shine, no noise. Communication: scheduled radio checks minimum every 2 hours.

Dead ground is terrain not visible from a specific viewpoint — it can conceal friendly or enemy movement. Identifying dead ground: look at the ground between you and a distant point — any hollow, reverse slope, or depression is potential dead ground. Exploitation: use dead ground to approach enemy positions unobserved. Counter-dead-ground: position OPs and sentry posts to cover likely dead ground. Re-entrants (valleys running toward enemy positions) are classic dead ground used for infiltration. In Kargil, Pakistani infiltrators used dead ground extensively to occupy heights undetected by Indian positions.

chunks.text: Tracking is following a person or animal through terrain by reading signs. Track types: footprints (note tread pattern, depth indicating load carried, stride length indicating pace), crushed vegetation, broken branches, disturbed soil, blood spoor. Age of tracks: fresh tracks have sharp edges, moist soil, no insect activity within the track; older tracks have weathered edges, dried appearance. Gait analysis: normal walk shows alternating left-right prints; running shows longer stride and toe-dig; injured person may drag a foot. Counter-tracking: walk on hard surfaces, step on stones, backtrack then change direction, walk in water.

A hide is a concealed position for long-duration observation or sniping. Construction principles: site must have clear observation of target area, covered approach route, concealed exit route (different from entry). Types: scrape (quick, shallow depression), shell scrape (deeper, provides ballistic protection), deep hide (for multi-day occupation — includes overhead cover, sleeping area, waste management). Waste management in hide: all food waste, human waste must be bagged and removed — smell reveals position. Entry and exit: only in darkness, same approach route used to avoid creating visible track. Maintain routine to avoid silhouette against light.

Night navigation is significantly more challenging than day navigation. Techniques: pace counting (know how many paces equal 100m for you — typically 62-66 double paces on flat ground), use of stars (Polaris/North Star is a fixed reference), handrails (linear features — roads, rivers, ridgelines — followed to a destination), attack points (obvious features near objective used as final navigation reference). Reduced speed: night navigation should be planned at 1/3 daytime speed. Red light torches preserve night vision (takes 20-30 minutes for eyes to fully adapt to darkness). NVDs impair depth perception — move slowly and deliberately.

River crossings are dangerous — more soldiers historically have died crossing rivers than in many battles. Assessment: check current speed (throw a stick — fast current = dangerous), depth (probe with pole), banks (steep banks indicate fast deep water), crossing point (widest = shallowest and slowest). Techniques: individual crossing — face upstream, lean on pole, move at 45° downstream angle, unclip pack straps and loosen boots before crossing. Group crossing: line abreast facing upstream, hands on each other's shoulders for stability. Never cross in darkness unless operationally essential. If swept away: float on back, feet downstream to fend off rocks.

Indian Army uses several grenade types. HE Fragmentation (36M): delay fuze 4-5 seconds, lethal radius 10m, danger area 100m, used against personnel in the open and in buildings. Smoke (L83): used for concealment and signalling. White Phosphorus (WP): incendiary and smoke, causes severe burns, burns underwater, used to clear bunkers and create smoke screens. Throwing technique: straighten pin (do not pull with finger — use thumb), firm grip, throw like a cricket ball, take cover immediately. Never cook a grenade (hold it before throwing to reduce reaction time — training accidents result). In confined spaces: stairwells and corridors create lethal overpressure.

The Under Barrel Grenade Launcher (UBGL) is attached to the INSAS or AK-203 rifle, firing 40mm grenades. Effective range: 150-300m. Minimum safe range: 30m (grenades arm after a certain spin count — will not explode if fired too close). Types of 40mm rounds: HE (fragmentation), smoke, illumination, rubber baton (riot control). The UBGL gives a rifle section indirect fire capability at section level. Loading: break open launcher, insert round, close — the trigger is separate from the rifle trigger. Point of aim: use the ladder sight, adjust for range. Clearance: treat a misfired round with extreme caution — wait 30 seconds, remove carefully.

The Nag is India's indigenous third-generation fire-and-forget Anti-Tank Guided Missile. Guidance: imaging infrared (IIR) seeker — locks onto heat signature of tank before launch and tracks autonomously (true fire and forget). Warhead: tandem HEAT — defeats ERA (Explosive Reactive Armour). Variants: Nag (ground launched from NAMICA vehicle), Helina/Dhruvastra (helicopter launched from HAL Rudra and LCH). Range: ground variant 0.5-4km, helicopter variant 7-10km. The missile can attack tank top armour (most vulnerable) in top-attack mode. Successfully completed development trials; induction into Indian Army ongoing.

The Spike ATGM is an Israeli missile system procured by India for infantry anti-armour capability. Variants: Spike-SR (short range, 800m), Spike-MR (medium range, 2.5km), Spike-LR (long range, 4km), Spike-ER (extended range, 8km). Guidance: electro-optical/infrared — man in the loop guidance allows operator to redirect missile in flight and abort if civilians detected. Tandem HEAT warhead defeats all known tank armour. Can be fired from shoulder, vehicle, or helicopter. India procured Spike-MR for infantry units and Spike-LR for helicopters. Advantage over older wire-guided systems: fire and steer, not fire and forget — greater targeting flexibility.

Man-Portable Air Defence Systems (MANPADS) provide infantry units with protection against low-flying aircraft and helicopters. Indian Army uses Igla-S (Russian) and Mistral (French). Igla-S: infrared heat-seeking, range 6km, altitude up to 3.5km, all-aspect engagement capability. Mistral: radar proximity fuze, range 6km, high agility for engaging fast jets. Employment: minimum two launchers per engagement (to counter evasive action), predict aircraft position (lead the target), verify identification before firing (IFF — Identification Friend or Foe is critical). Avoid using near own aircraft corridors. Backblast: minimum 25m clearance behind launcher.

The Bofors FH77B 155mm howitzer is one of the most effective artillery pieces in Indian Army service. Range: 30km with extended range ammunition, 40km+ with Excalibur GPS-guided rounds. Rate of fire: burst 3 rounds in 8 seconds, sustained 2-3 rpm. Crew: 8-10 soldiers. Accuracy: the Bofors was decisive in the 1999 Kargil War — its ability to fire at high angles allowed it to engage Pakistani positions on reverse slopes of very high peaks. Counter-battery fire: the Bofors' survivability comes from rapid displacement after firing (shoot and scoot). Ammunition types: HE, smoke, illumination, Cargo (sub-munitions), Excalibur precision.

Pinaka is India's indigenous multi-barrel rocket system (MBRS), equivalent to the Russian BM-21 Grad or US MLRS. A battery of 6 Pinaka launchers can fire 72 rockets in 44 seconds. Mark I: range 37.5km. Mark II: range 65km. Mark III (guided): range 75km+ with GPS/INS guidance. Warhead types: HE, incendiary, anti-tank sub-munitions, mine-laying. Pinaka is highly mobile — mounted on Tatra truck. Used for area saturation, counter-battery, and deep interdiction missions. Inducted into Indian Army and operated by artillery regiments. Exported to Armenia (used in Nagorno-Karabakh conflict).

Combat engineers (Sappers in Indian Army — Corps of Engineers) support infantry with: mobility (breaching obstacles, building bridges), counter-mobility (minefield laying, demolitions), survivability (field fortifications, bunker construction). Bangalore torpedo: metal tube filled with explosive, used to breach wire obstacles and clear mine lanes — sections pushed together and detonated. Demolitions: C4 plastic explosive — 1.5x more powerful than TNT by weight, shaped charges for cutting steel, cratering charges for denying roads. Mine marking: standard mine markers must be clearly visible from standing height. Never remove markers.

A well-constructed field fortification can multiply the fighting power of a small unit. Shell scrape: individual protection from direct fire and shell fragments, dug quickly (30-45 minutes for two soldiers). Fire trench: deeper than shell scrape, allows fighting while remaining protected, headcover added. Sandbag construction: each layer offset by half a bag from layer below (stretcher bond), minimum 4 layers for protection from small arms, 8 layers for mortar fragments. Overhead cover requires minimum 30cm compacted earth over timber supports to stop mortar fragments. Drainage: all trenches must drain or they fill with rainwater during monsoon.

Anti-tank and anti-personnel minefields must be breached for attacking forces to pass through. Methods: manual (prodding with bayonet at 30° angle every 10cm — slow but reliable), mechanical (mine roller or flail attachment on vehicles), explosive (Bangalore torpedo or line charge). Minefield recording: record mine type, location (grid and distance from markers), density, and fuze type. Gaps in a minefield must be minimum 8m wide for vehicles, 2m wide for infantry. Mark breached lanes clearly with tape or pickets. When in doubt — probe. A missed mine can kill an entire section. Mine-awareness training is mandatory.

Electronic Warfare (EW) involves three elements: Electronic Surveillance (ES — listening to enemy signals), Electronic Attack (EA — jamming enemy communications), Electronic Protection (EP — protecting own signals). Signs of enemy jamming: sudden increase in noise/static on radio, unable to communicate on usual frequency. Counter-jamming: change frequency (frequency hopping radios do this automatically), increase power, reposition antenna, use alternate communication means (messenger, signal panels). EMCON (Emission Control): strict radio silence to deny enemy signals intelligence. Mobile phones emit radio signals continuously — a significant SIGINT vulnerability even when not making calls.

Field telephone systems provide secure communication without the radio emission vulnerability. D-10 field cable can be run up to 5km per reel. Wire laying: run along one side of the road, mark clearly to prevent vehicle damage, cross roads underground if possible. Telephone exchange (field): connects multiple lines. Code: all positions and persons referred to by codename — never use real names or locations on field telephone. Advantages over radio: cannot be intercepted by direction-finding equipment, no frequency allocation needed, no battery-critical radio required. Disadvantage: wire can be cut by enemy, takes time to lay.

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are now common in modern warfare including the India-Pakistan and India-China contexts. Indian Army uses: Heron (strategic surveillance), Searcher Mk II (tactical surveillance), Rustom-2 (MALE UAV under development), small quadcopters for section-level reconnaissance. Enemy drone threats: quadcopters for surveillance, fixed-wing for strike. Signs of enemy drone: buzzing sound (quadcopter), thermal signature on NVDs, visual sighting. Counter-drone measures: electronic jamming (disrupts GPS control link), kinetic (shooting — requires permission), net guns (for small drones). Always report unidentified aerial objects. Avoid using mobile phones or active radios when drone is suspected overhead.

Cyber threats to soldiers in the field include: social engineering (fake contacts on social media gathering operational information), phishing (fake emails/messages with malicious links), SIM cloning (mobile number duplicated to intercept calls). Operational security on social media: never post unit movements, troop positions, equipment details, or deployment timings. Even seemingly harmless photos can reveal location through metadata and background details. Password security: strong passwords (12+ characters, mix of types), never share passwords, change regularly. Official communication only through secured government networks. Report suspicious digital activity to the unit signals officer immediately.

The Para Special Forces (Para SF) are India's elite special operations forces, drawn from the Parachute Regiment. Selection: gruelling probation course with very high attrition rate — candidates must complete a long-distance solo navigation exercise with minimal rations. Roles: direct action, special reconnaissance, hostage rescue, counter-terrorism, foreign internal defence. Units: 1 Para SF, 2 Para SF, 3 Para SF, 4 Para SF, 9 Para SF, 10 Para SF, 21 Para SF. Para SF conducted Operation Sunrise cross-border strikes in Myanmar (2015) and surgical strikes across LOC in Pakistan (2016). Equipped with: Glock 17, M4 carbine, SIG716, various specialist weapons.

MARCOS (Marine Commandos) are the Indian Navy's special operations force, considered among India's most elite units. Selection process lasts 3 years. Roles: maritime counter-terrorism, underwater demolition, ship seizure, beach reconnaissance, anti-piracy. Training: HALO/HAHO parachuting, combat diving, close quarter battle, VBSS (Visit Board Search and Seizure). MARCOS were deployed in the 2008 Mumbai attacks (26/11) — cleared terrorists from the boat MV Kuber and assisted in other operations. Equipped with: Tavor TAR-21, MP5, HK33, underwater weapons, various diving equipment. The MARCOS motto is 'The Few, The Fearless'.

The Garud Commando Force is the Indian Air Force's special operations unit. Primary roles: airfield seizure and defence, CSAR (Combat Search and Rescue) of downed pilots, counter-terrorism at air force bases, and support to other special operations. Selection is highly competitive, drawing from existing IAF personnel. Training includes airborne operations, combat diving, close quarter battle, SERE (Survival, Evasion, Resistance, Escape). Garud units are permanently positioned at key IAF bases for airfield defence. During the 2019 Balakot air strikes, Garud units were on standby for CSAR operations in case any IAF pilot was downed in Pakistani territory.

Logistics in the Indian Army follows the principle: 'Amateurs talk strategy, professionals talk logistics.' Supply classes: Class I (food and water), Class II (clothing and equipment), Class III (fuel and lubricants), Class IV (construction materials), Class V (ammunition), Class VIII (medical supplies). Ammunition resupply: units maintain a basic load (day of fire) and are resupplied based on consumption. High-altitude resupply: Siachen posts receive supplies primarily by helicopter (Cheetah and ALH Dhruv) as road access is impossible. Air maintenance (air dropping) used when helicopter landing is not possible. Water forward to troops in desert and high altitude is a critical logistics task.

In forward areas, soldiers may need to cook their own food using field cooking sets. Importance of hot meals for morale — Unit commanders are responsible for ensuring troops receive hot food when operationally possible. Water resupply: reverse osmosis water purification units (ROWPU) can purify 1,500 litres per hour from any water source — unit level capability. Jerrycan discipline: fuel and water jerrycans are different colours — never mix them. Forward water points: established as close to troops as possible. In desert operations (Rajasthan), water discipline is mission-critical — soldiers must carry minimum 4 litres. Camel-back hydration systems increasingly issued.

Calling for artillery fire is a critical skill. Fire mission format: Warning order ('Fire mission'), Target location (grid 6-8 digit), Target description, Method of engagement, Method of fire and control. Observer adjustments: the observer sees where the first round lands and adjusts: ADD (increase range), DROP (decrease range), LEFT/RIGHT (in metres), UP (elevation). Danger close: when friendly troops are within 600m of target (artillery) — must be declared explicitly. Lifting fire: 'LIFT' when friendly troops are about to assault through target area. Shifts: 'SHIFT, direction, distance'. Key principle: artillery kills through fragmentation — soldiers must be in cover during friendly artillery.

Close Air Support (CAS) is air-delivered fire in close proximity to friendly forces. Requesting CAS: pilot must know your position before target location (to avoid fratricide). 9-Line CAS brief: IP (Initial Point), Heading to target, Distance, Target elevation, Target description, Target location, Type mark (smoke, laser, IR strobe), Location of friendlies, Egress direction. Laser designation: laser target designator marks target for laser-guided bombs. Fratricide prevention: VS-17 signal panels, IR strobes (visible only on NVDs), coloured smoke. Minimum safe distance for CAS: depends on aircraft type and munition — coordinate with the pilot. Mark your position before calling CAS.

Hostage rescue is one of the most dangerous military tasks. Principles: speed, surprise, and violence of action — hesitation costs lives. Phases: intelligence gathering, planning, rehearsal, insertion, assault, extraction. Assault: simultaneous entry through multiple points to prevent hostages being used as shields, achieve dominance in under 30 seconds. Shoot/no-shoot: positive identification of target before firing — hostages and terrorists will be mixed together in the dark and chaos. Flashbang (stun grenade) disorients occupants without lethal effect — 2-3 seconds of disorientation window. After assault: immediate medical aid to all casualties, account for all hostages.

The National Security Guard (NSG) is India's premier federal counter-terrorism force, under Ministry of Home Affairs. Nicknamed 'Black Cats' for their black uniforms. Two elements: Special Action Group (SAG — military personnel on secondment) and Special Ranger Group (SRG — police personnel). Role: counter-terrorism, hostage rescue, VIP protection, IED disposal, aircraft hijacking response. NSG conducted Operation Black Tornado during 26/11 Mumbai attacks (2008) — clearing the Taj Hotel, Trident Hotel, and Nariman House. HQ: Manesar, Haryana, with hubs in Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata, and Hyderabad. NSG also manages the National Bomb Data Centre.

The HAL Tejas is India's indigenously developed light combat aircraft (LCA), inducted into the Indian Air Force in 2016. Engine: GE F404 (Mark 1), GE F414 (Mark 2 — more powerful). Speed: Mach 1.8. Weapons: R-73 AAM (dogfight), Derby/Astra BVR AAMs, bombs, rockets, gun (23mm twin-barrel). Fly-by-wire flight control system makes it inherently unstable for better agility. Mark 2 will have AESA radar, more powerful engine, air-to-air refuelling capability, and carrier suitability. The Navy variant (Tejas NMR) is under development for INS Vikrant. India is the 6th country to develop a supersonic fly-by-wire combat aircraft indigenously.

The HAL Advanced Light Helicopter (ALH) Dhruv is a twin-engine multi-role helicopter developed and manufactured indigenously by HAL. Variants: Dhruv (utility/transport), ALH-WSI Rudra (armed — guns, rockets, Helina missiles), LCH (Light Combat Helicopter — dedicated attack). Engine: Shakti (indigenous development of Turbomeca TM333). Speed: 290 km/h. Range: 350km. Ceiling: 6,000m (critical for high-altitude operations in Ladakh and Siachen). Dhruv operates in extreme conditions — has operated at altitudes exceeding 8,000m. Equipped with: EFIS glass cockpit, NVD-compatible lighting, flotation gear for maritime variant. Used extensively for CASEVAC in high-altitude postings.

Indian Air Force operates several fast jet types. Su-30 MKI (primary air superiority fighter): twin-engine, supermaneuverable, range 3,000km, carries BrahMos-A air-launched cruise missile. Mirage 2000 (precision strike): laser-guided bombs, SCALP cruise missile — used in Balakot 2019 airstrikes. MiG-29 (fleet air defence): phased out and upgraded versions with Indian Navy (MiG-29K from INS Vikramaditya). Rafale (inducted 2020): Meteor BVR missile (range 100km+), SCALP cruise missile, SPECTRA electronic warfare suite — currently most capable IAF fighter. Jaguar (ground attack): being phased out. F-21 and MQ-9B under consideration for future induction.

INS Vikrant (IAC-1) is India's first indigenously built aircraft carrier, commissioned in September 2022. Displacement: 45,000 tonnes (full load). Length: 262m. Aircraft capacity: up to 30 aircraft (MiG-29K fighters, Ka-31 AEW helicopters, MH-60R ASW helicopters, ALH Dhruv). STOBAR (Short Take-Off But Arrested Recovery) configuration — ski-jump for takeoff, arrestor wires for landing. Propulsion: 4 General Electric LM2500 gas turbines, 88MW total power, speed 28 knots. Manufactured at Cochin Shipyard. Steel hull made from Indian-produced DMR 249A special grade steel. Represents a major milestone in India's indigenous defence manufacturing.

Indian Navy operates conventional and nuclear submarines. Conventional (diesel-electric): Kalvari class (6 Scorpene-type — French design, indigenous build at MDL Mumbai), Shishumar class (German Type 209, aging). Nuclear: INS Arihant (SSBN — ballistic missile submarine, carries K-15 SLBMs), INS Arighat (second SSBN commissioned 2024), INS Chakra (nuclear attack submarine — leased from Russia). Submarine stealth: extremely quiet, difficult to detect. Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) against them: P-8I Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft, helicopter sonobuoys, ship-mounted sonar, torpedoes. Future: 6 additional conventional submarines under P-75I project.

The 1971 war resulted in the creation of Bangladesh from East Pakistan. Indian Army launched a swift 13-day campaign (December 3-16, 1971) coordinated across four fronts. Key operations: capture of Dhaka, amphibious landing at Cox's Bazar, airborne assault by 2 Para Battalion at Tangail (one of India's few combat airborne operations). Pakistan's Eastern Command surrendered on December 16 — the largest military surrender since World War II (93,000 POWs). Indian Navy blockaded East Pakistan, INS Vikrant ensured no escape by sea. Chief of Army Staff: General S.H.F.J. Manekshaw (later promoted to Field Marshal). The war is studied as a model of joint operations.

The 1962 Sino-Indian War was a significant military defeat that shaped Indian Army doctrine. Background: border dispute over McMahon Line (Arunachal Pradesh) and Aksai Chin. Key battles: Namka Chu, Rezang La (Major Shaitan Singh's Charlie Company — 114 soldiers held against thousands of Chinese, all killed, posthumous PVC to Shaitan Singh), Se La Pass. Lessons learned: inadequate logistics and supply to forward posts, political interference in military decisions, poor equipment (World War II era), lack of high-altitude warfare training. Post-1962 reforms: formation of high-altitude warfare units, significant investment in border infrastructure (now being accelerated under BRO), Corps of Mountain Artillery established.

Operation Parakram was the largest military mobilisation in India since 1971, triggered by the terrorist attack on the Indian Parliament (December 13, 2001, carried out by Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed). India mobilised approximately 500,000 troops to the Pakistan border. The standoff lasted approximately 10 months without leading to open war. Lessons from the mobilisation: the time taken to mobilise (weeks rather than days) revealed need for a Cold Start / Pro-Active Operations doctrine allowing faster mobilisation of smaller strike formations. The operation also revealed gaps in equipment, especially tank ammunition stocks, mine-clearing capability, and medical infrastructure along the Pakistan border.

India's military gallantry awards (in order of precedence): Param Vir Chakra (PVC) — highest, awarded for most conspicuous bravery in presence of enemy, only 21 awarded since independence (all but one posthumously). Maha Vir Chakra (MVC) — second highest, conspicuous gallantry in the presence of the enemy. Vir Chakra (VrC) — third, acts of bravery in the presence of the enemy. Ashok Chakra — highest peacetime gallantry (equivalent to PVC), awarded for gallantry not in the presence of the enemy. Kirti Chakra and Shaurya Chakra follow. Sena Medal, Nau Sena Medal, Vayu Sena Medal — service-specific for lesser acts of gallantry. Vishist Seva Medal for distinguished service.

The Indian Army maintains a regimental system inherited from the British, with strong regimental identity and traditions. Major infantry regiments: Brigade of Guards, Punjab Regiment, Grenadiers, Maratha Light Infantry, Rajput Regiment, Sikh Regiment, Sikh Light Infantry, Dogra Regiment, Garhwal Rifles, Kumaon Regiment, Assam Regiment, Bihar Regiment, Mahar Regiment, JAT Regiment, Rajputana Rifles, Naga Regiment, Ladakh Scouts. Each regiment has distinct traditions, cap badges, and recruiting areas. The regimental system builds fierce unit loyalty (izzat) which motivates soldiers in battle. Gurkha Rifles (5 regiments remaining with Indian Army) maintain Nepalese recruitment.

Indian Army support arms and services: Corps of Engineers (Sappers and Miners — motto 'Sarvatra' meaning Everywhere), Corps of Signals, Army Aviation Corps, Army Air Defence, Army Service Corps (logistics), Army Medical Corps, Army Ordnance Corps, Army Education Corps, Judge Advocate General's Branch, Remount and Veterinary Corps (horses and mules still used in high altitude), Military Nursing Service, Corps of Military Police. Armoured Corps (tanks and mechanised forces). Artillery (Regiment of Artillery). Intelligence Corps. Each arm and service has distinct training centres: Engineers at Pune, Signals at Jabalpur, Artillery at Nasik Road/Devlali.
